Abstract The clinical and neurophysiological findings in
a patient with a typical stiff-man syndrome and their three-
year evolution are described. The patient had high titers of
anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies in both serum
and cerebrospinal fluid. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
of brain and spinal cord was normal. Transcranial magnetic
stimulation (TMS) revealed a distinctive motor evoked
potential (MEP) pattern in proximal lower limb muscles
consisting of markedly increased MEP amplitudes and
MEP/M ratios, reduced excitability thresholds, and absent
silent period. However, MEP latencies, central and peripher-
al conduction times and amplitudes obtained by magnetic
spinal root stimulation were normal. Treatment with benzo-
diazepine and baclofen normalized both the clinical picture
and the MEP values. TMS may be useful both as a diagnos-
tic tool and to monitor the response to drug treatment.

Case report
Clinical picture
In December 1995, a 37-year-old woman gave a 9-month
history of slowly progressive backache, stiffness, aching
and painful muscle spasms of both lower limbs. Her family
and past medical histories were unremarkable. Evaluation
revealed mild scoliosis and severe lordosis of the thora-
columbar spine, persisting at rest. The lower half of the
trunk and proximal lower limb muscles were symmetrically
stiff, and passive stretching or light touch of the extremities
provoked painful repetitive muscle spasms. V oluntary
movements of the trunk and legs were awkward and restrict-
ed. She required assistance to walk because of lower limb
muscle stiffness and superimposed severe spasms in affect-
ed muscles. Spasms lasting up to several minutes recurred
spontaneously or were evoked by sudden noises, somato-
sensory stimuli, emotional stress. Cognition, cranial nerves,

muscle strength, tendon reflexes, coordination, sensation
and sphincter functions were normal. Investigations were
performed with the approval of the local ethics committee
and the consent of the patient.
Neuroimaging and laboratory investigations
Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the head
and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head and
spine were normal. A detailed biochemical investigation
gave normal results with regard to the following parame-
ters: full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function,
creatine kinase, blood glucose, serum vitamin B12, serum
levels of IgG, IgA, IgM, complement factors C3 and C4,
free T3 and T4, TSH, serum protein immunofixation, oral
glucose tolerance test, search for antinuclear and anti-
acetylcholine receptor autoantibodies, neoplastic markers,
serological investigations for viral and bacterial agents, and
cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) parameters including cell count,
total protein, IgG content and IgG index. Oligoclonal bands
were absent. 
The following autoantibodies were detected: anti-islet
cell antibodies were present both in serum and CSF (nor-
mal: none), thyroid microsomial antibody titer was 1:2518
(normal: <1:50), and thyroid thyroglobulin antibody titer
1:437 (normal: <1:100). Samples of serum and CSF were
characterized by autoantibodies to glutamic acid decar-
boxylase (GAD-Ab). Both serum and CSF were positive in
radiobinding assays for GAD-Ab (isoform 65) (>100 U,
normal: <5 U). Using an immunocytochemical technique
high titers of autoantibodies against GABAergic neurons
were demonstrated both in serum and CSF. With
immunoblot both serum and CSF samples recognized a
band with the same electrophoretic mobility as GAD [6, 7]. 
Electrophysiological studies
Nerve conduction studies (NCS) were performed with
supramaximal percutaneous nerve stimulation and surface
electrode recording according to standard techniques using
a Viking IIe (Madison, Wisconsin). Median, femoral, per-
oneal and sural nerves were examined on both sides. 
Electromyography (EMG) was performed using a pair
of 10-mm diameter Ag/AgCl electrodes placed 2-4 cm apart
longitudinally over the muscle bellies and standard Medelec
concentric needle electrodes. The following muscles were
bilaterally examined: deltoideus, biceps brachii, flexor carpi
radialis, thenar muscles, lumbar paraspinal muscles, gluteus
maximus, hamstrings, quadriceps, tibialis anterior and gas-
trocnemius-soleus complex. Short latency median and poste-
rior tibial nerve somatosensory evoked potentials were
recorded on both sides according to the recommendations of
134
the IFCN Committee [9]. Long latency reflexes (LLRs) were
elicited in leg muscles according to previously described
methods [10]. Electroencephalogram (EEG) registered using
the international 10-20 electrode system with standard con-
ditions.
Noninvasive magnetic stimulation of the brain and spinal
roots was performed according to the procedures suggested
by Rossini et al. [11], using a 14-cm outer diameter, flat
round coil powered by Novametrix Magstim 200. The sub-
ject was lying supine in a comfortable position, and was
mentally relaxed with both eyes closed. Signals were ampli-
fied and filtered with a band pass of 10-5000 Hz.
Quantitative analysis of EMG responses was carried out off-
line using the Viking IIe. EMG responses were recorded
from biceps brachii (BB), abductor digiti minimi (ADM),
tibialis anterior (TA) and vastus medialis (VM) muscles

using a pair of 10-mm diameter Ag/AgCl surface electrodes
in a belly-tendon montage. Muscles were examined at rest
and during a slight sustained voluntary contraction of about
20% of maximal isometric force (MIF) of the target muscle
(as controlled by EMG recordings), giving the patient visual
and auditory feed-back of EMG activity to assist her in main-
taining either complete relaxation or the correct amount of
activation. Cortical stimulation was performed at 40% above
each muscle resting motor threshold (T). The center of the
coil was placed on the vertex with the current flowing clock-
wise (as viewed from above). Because of continuous motor
unit activity (CMUA) and the difficulty in obtaining reliable
F wave in proximal muscles such as VM and BB, central
conduction time (CCT) was measured by subtracting the
peripheral conduction time estimated by direct stimulation of
the efferent roots over the vertebral column from the total
latency of MEPs. MEP amplitude was measured peak-to-
peak and was also expressed in terms of percentage of the
muscle response amplitude evoked by TMS compared to that
obtained by supramaximal percutaneous electrical peripher-
al nerve stimulation (ulnar nerve at wrist for ADM, muscu-
locutaneous nerve at Erb’s point for BB, femoral nerve just
below the inguinal ligament for VM, peroneal nerve at the
knee for TA) (MEP/M); care was taken to obtain the maxi-
mal M response, moving the active electrode if necessary. In
this way we obtained an approximation of the percentage of
the motorneuron pool activated by scalp stimulation. Ten
responses were recorded for each muscle and measurements
were made of the shortest onset latency and the largest
amplitude. Silent period (SP) was obtained from VM and TA
muscles during a tonic muscular activation of about 20% of
MIF. Stimulus intensity was 140% of T. Duration of SP was
measured (in ms) from the end of the MEP to the first reap-
pearing burst of the EMG activity. Four recordings were
superimposed and the shortest SP was determined. Results
were compared with normative values (mean ± SD) obtained
in 20 healthy subjects (18-50 years old) and the observed
values were considered abnormal when they were beyond ±
2 SD of normal mean. 
F. Logullo et al.: MEP in stiff-man syndrome

Our patient fulfills the clinical and electrophysiological cri-
teria of Lorish and colleagues [1] for SMS. It is quite con-
troversial whether SMS is a homogenous clinical entity or
rather a heterogenous syndrome [2, 12] and recently the
range of clinical expression of SMS has been reviewed
[13]. When the patients are selected in strict accordance
with Lorish’s evolution of Gordon and co-workers guide-
lines [1, 14], SMS appears to be a quite homogenous enti-
ty with a high incidence of anti-GAD and other organ-spe-
cific autoantibodies. Our patient belongs to the “typical”
SMS subgroup. Although in our patient the symptoms were
prominent in the legs, involvement of the thoracolumbar
muscles and the presence of GAD-Ab differentiated our
patient even from those with “stiff leg syndrome” described
by Brown et al. [15]. Recently a “focal” form of SMS has
been described in two patients with high titer of GAD-Ab,
but their stiffness and spasms were limited to one leg, spar-
ing the trunk [16]. 
A variety of drugs has been tried for symptomatic treat-
ment of SMS [3]. In our patient the association benzodi-
136
azepine-baclofen, both with GABAergic action, turned out
more effective than the combination benzodiazepine and
tizanidine, a centrally acting alpha-adrenergic agonist,
probably for the synergistic action of benzodiazepine and
baclofen. Because of the benign course, immunosuppres-
sive therapy was not carried out. 
Clinical, electrophysiological and pharmacological data
suggest that the physiopathological basis of SMS consists in
an unbalanced excitatory and inhibitory input onto spinal
motorneurons [4]. GAD-Ab may cause an immune-mediated
inhibition of GABAergic neuron function, thus determining
an abnormal excitability of spinal and/or supraspinal (brain-
stem, cortical) interneuronal networks [7].
Data about TMS in SMS are scanty. In the patients
described by Meinck et al. [8], magnetic brain stimulation
yielded unremarkable results but data were not given in
detail. Schulte-Mattler and Zeirz [17] reported an SMS
patient who showed characteristic, abnormal late responses
(LRs) upon TMS. The amplitude of the LRs corresponded
with the symptoms and the LRs were symptomatic of SMS.
Quatrale et al. [18] reported in abstract form abnormality of
the muscle silent period induced by transcranial cortical
stimulation in 5 patients with SMS. In our patient magnet-
ic stimulation of the brain and the spinal roots revealed in
involved muscles a distinctive pattern pointing to structur-
al integrity of the corticospinal tract and a spinal alpha-
motorneuron hyperexcitability: normal central conduction
time, reduced excitability thresholds, cortically elicited
MEPs of increased amplitude but of normal morphology
along with normal MEPs on spinal root stimulation, and
absent or reduced SP. TMS excitability thresholds and MEP
amplitude normalized as the clinical picture improved,
while abnormally short VM SP persisted. Because TMS

excites all or nearly all spinal alpha-motorneurons inner-
vating a target muscle in healthy subjects [19], the very
large MEP amplitudes in our patient when untreated are
probably due to a reduced or absent desynchronization that
in “conventional” TMS normally occurs within the corti-
cospinal tract and/or at spinal cell level. Thus, in SMS all
spinal motorneurons leading to the involved muscles,
because of their hyperexcitability (as demonstrated also by
LLRs), achieve synchronous depolarization, minimizing
MEP phase cancellation and greatly enhancing MEP ampli-
tude. The available MEP data do not reveal the level (spinal
and/or supraspinal) at which the neurophysiological dys-
functions responsible for stiff-man syndrome are located.
Spinal alpha-motorneuron hyperexcitability may result
both from abnormal excitability of spinal neuronal net-
works alone and from increased excitatory/reduced
inhibitory supraspinal drive. Moreover, the GAD-Ab medi-
ated disinhibition may be unevenly distributed, mainly
involving the thoracolumbosacral cord, as in our patient,
but not completely sparing supraspinal structures (as sug-
gested by her disrupted sleep pattern) or may involve wide-
ly the CNS, such as in the patient described by Martinelli et
al. [20]. 
We conclude that in SMS, TMS may be useful both as a
diagnostic tool and to monitor the evolution of the disease
and the response to drug treatment.
